summary: Defines several structured syntax suffixes for media type names, namely +json, +ber, +der, +fastinfoset, +wbxml and +zip. A suffix tells software the underlying format, so generic tools can handle specialized types. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A media type can name a specialized kind of content and also show its underlying format with a suffix such as +json. Software can use that suffix when it only needs to handle the format itself. This document defines several suffixes and explains their registration rules.

subtitle: Structured suffixes identify the underlying format in a media type name.

tldr.problem: A specialized media type can have useful meaning of its own while still using a familiar underlying data format. Without a shared suffix convention, general-purpose software may not recognize that format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6839 defines and registers the +json, +ber, +der, +fastinfoset, +wbxml, and +zip suffixes, and provides the registration for +xml. It also describes how suffix and media-type rules apply to fragment identifiers.
tldr.outcome: The suffix can let software process the underlying representation when it does not need the specialized meaning. This RFC updates RFC 3023 and has been updated by RFC 7303.

today: RFC 6839 is Informational. It updates RFC 3023 and has itself been updated by RFC 7303.

sections.title: What a Structured Syntax Suffix Tells You
sections.content:
A media type may have specialized semantics while its representation follows a known format. The +xml convention in RFC 3023 was an earlier example: a type ending in +xml uses XML underneath.

RFC 6839 defines and registers +json, +ber, +der, +fastinfoset, +wbxml, and +zip. It also supplies a registration form for +xml under the structured syntax suffix procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The suffix at the end of a media type name can identify the format used inside it. A program can use that information when it does not need the type's special meaning.

sections.title: When Generic Processing Is Appropriate
sections.content:
A structured suffix is appropriate when the specific media type has meaning beyond its underlying representation. The suffix lets a receiver use general processing only if it does not need the specialized meaning and can parse the format without extra knowledge.

The suffix does not erase the specific media type. It identifies a shared representation so that tools which need only that representation can handle it.
sections.plainLanguage: A general-purpose tool can use the suffix when it only needs to read the underlying format. It still needs specialized handling when the media type's particular meaning matters.

sections.title: The Registered Suffixes
sections.content:
+json identifies JSON representation. +ber and +der identify the Basic and Distinguished Encoding Rules; +fastinfoset identifies a binary representation of the XML Information Set; +wbxml identifies WAP Binary XML; and +zip identifies the ZIP storage and transfer format.

The registrations describe encoding considerations and refer to security considerations for each underlying format. For example, the BER and DER registrations warn about invalid length fields and deep nesting. The RFC separately provides a registration for +xml.
sections.plainLanguage: The suffixes name formats such as JSON, two ASN.1 encodings, two binary XML formats, and ZIP. Their registrations also point readers to format-specific security concerns.

sections.title: How Fragment Identifiers Are Processed
sections.content:
For a media type such as type/subtype+suffix, a fragment identifier is first handled under the suffix's rules when those rules define it and resolve it. If the suffix rules do not define or resolve the fragment, the specific media type's rules apply.

The registration for +xml follows the fragment rules that RFC 3023 gave for application/xml. RFC 6839 warns that changing generic suffix rules can conflict with rules for individual media types.
sections.plainLanguage: A fragment points to part of a resource. The suffix rules apply when they cover that fragment; otherwise, the specific media type's rules decide how to handle it.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility of Suffix Rules
sections.content:
Individual media types can add security concerns beyond those in a suffix registration. BER and DER use type-length-value structures; invalid lengths can cause buffer overruns, and arbitrary nesting can cause stack overflows.

Generic fragment rules take precedence over media-type-specific rules. Changing a suffix's rules can therefore affect existing registrations and software, creating interoperability or security problems. The RFC says to review affected media types before changing a suffix registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs that read BER or DER need to check lengths and nesting. Changing suffix rules can affect existing types, so the RFC calls for reviewing those effects first.
